papers.title: EEG signature in psychiatrist's subjective experience: a pilot study.
papers.abstract: The Assessment of Clinician's Subjective Experience (ACSE) is a self-report questionnaire developed to evaluate clinicians' subjective experiences during patient interactions. While its psychometric properties and clinical validity have been supported, its neurobiological correlates have not yet been investigated. In this pilot study, two clinicians and ten patients participated in a three-phase protocol comprising: (1) a first clinical interview, (2) ACSE administration, and (3) listening to the audio recording of the first clinical interview. EEG activity was recorded from clinicians during both the first clinical interview and questionnaire administration. Neural data were analyzed in terms of relative power spectral density, node strength, and global efficiency computed from imaginary coherence. Clinicians were psychiatrists, one male and one female. Seven patients were diagnosed with mixed anxiety and depressive disorder, and three with unspecified anxiety disorders. ACSE scores were highest for the Difficulty in attunement and Engagement dimensions, consistent with previous literature. EEG findings revealed dimension-specific and topographically distinct oscillatory patterns for only two ACSE dimensions: Difficulty in Attunement and Engagement. More limited evidence emerged for Disconfirmation. Functional connectivity analyses indicated different network profiles, characterized by differences in global efficiency patterns. Correlational analyses further identified significant associations between ACSE dimensions and EEG-derived features. These preliminary findings provide initial evidence that clinicians' subjective experiences during clinical encounters could be associated with measurable neural signatures, offering a novel perspective on the neurobiological basis of intersubjective processes in clinical settings.

papers.title: A feature-optimized EEG framework using multiscale entropy and metaheuristic optimization for cognitive analysis.
papers.abstract: Cognitive activity plays an important role by influencing working-memory, problem-solving, attention, response and decision making. EEG serves as a non-invasive approach to analyze neural activity associated with cognitive processing. The current study aims to identify the more contributing features to analyze the cognitive activity between sports and non-sports groups. The present study included 100 participants, consisting of 80 males and 20 females aged between 19 and 23 years. EEG signals were acquired and preprocessed using filtering methods to remove unwanted noise and artifacts. The four-entropy metrics dispersion entropy, permutation entropy, sample entropy, and fuzzy entropy were applied to the coarse-graining method across multiple temporal scales to analyze the complexity of EEG signals. To identify the most informative feature subsets and reduce redundancy, filter-based methods such as Mutual Information, Pearson Correlation, Minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance and wrapper-based methods such as Genetic Algorithm and Particle Swarm Optimization were applied. Finally for differentiating the cognitive activity, five machine learning classifiers that include Support Vector Machine, Artificial Neural Network, K-nearest neighbor, Decision Tree and Random Forest were applied. Statistical methods such as T-test and Fleiss kappa were used to analyse the performance efficiency. Feature extraction phase yielded a total of 160 multiscale entropy features. The entire features when fed into both filter-based and wrapper-based methods, Genetic Algorithm based optimization yielded a minimal contributing feature subset with high nested cross-validated accuracy of 93.0 ± 2.7% with Support Vector Machine. This contributing feature subset was used as input for five different machine learning classifiers for differentiating the cognitive activity between both groups. The five classifiers demonstrated high cross-validated agreement on held-out subjects, with a mean Fleiss' kappa of 0.874 ± 0.051 (95% CI: 0.811-0.937), depicting a good inter-classifier agreement for classification of samples into sports and non-sports individuals. The study demonstrates that multiscale entropy features combined with metaheuristic-based feature optimization can effectively analyze the cognitive activity between sports and non-sports individuals. The proposed EEG framework provides a structured approach for real-time cognitive activity analysis using compact and informative entropy-based feature subsets.

papers.title: Study protocol for microneurographic investigation of nociceptor sensitisation in fibromyalgia syndrome (MICRO-FMS).
papers.abstract: Chronic pain in fibromyalgia may be driven by abnormal ongoing activity in a subclass of C-fibre nociceptors known as Type1B or CMi nociceptors. As is common in C-nociceptor microneurography studies, the modest patient numbers in these prior studies generate large confidence intervals around the point estimate of the prevalence of this abnormal activity. This complicates the interpretation of the relative importance of this ongoing nociceptor activity as a pain generating mechanism in fibromyalgia. The study aims to improve precision via an adaptive Bayesian protocol that maximises the yield and quality of data collection whilst minimising patient burden. This study will clarify whether the prevalence of ongoing nociceptor activity is higher in the fibromyalgia patient population, and if this is correlated with their sensory phenotype and/or pain experience, providing much needed insight into the mechanisms of the condition. The study employs an optimised microneurography protocol with an adaptive study design. The microneurography protocol incorporates early identification of CMi nociceptors via an abbreviated activity dependent slowing protocol to increase yields enabling efficient collection of the primary outcome data. The adaptive study design will use Bayesian principles to iteratively assess the predictive probability of futility, and terminate early if there is high confidence that the hypothesis is false. Furthermore, the study will employ questionnaires to explore links with pain in the area under study to the electrophysiology data. Finally, quantitative sensory testing will be used to investigate whether the irritable nociceptor phenotype is associated with abnormalities in CMi nociceptor physiology. This study has received HRA REC approval in the UK. Participants will provide written informed consent, and may withdraw at any time without consequence. At the end of the study, the results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication, and the data made available via a data repository.

Sleep stage-specific heart rate variability feature-driven clustering analysis: identifying cardiac autonomic endotypes with long-term cardiovascular predictive value.
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular risk assessment in obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) has traditionally relied on the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI). However, AHI primarily reflects respiratory event burden and may not adequately capture inter-individual heterogeneity in sleep-related cardiorespiratory regulation. This study aimed to identify sleep stage-specific heart rate variability (HRV) phenotypes and evaluate their associations with long-term cardiovascular outcomes. Data were obtained from the Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS). After exclusion of participants with missing clinical covariates or outcome data, 4029 individuals were included. Linear and non-linear HRV features were extracted from stage-specific electrocardiographic segments during N2, N3, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. K-means clustering was performed independently for each sleep stage after Z-score standardization, and the optimal cluster number was determined using silhouette coefficients and the elbow method. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models and Kaplan-Meier analyses were used to evaluate associations between HRV-informed phenotypes and all-cause mortality, coronary heart disease, and cardiovascular disease (CVD). Three HRV-informed phenotypes were identified within the selected clustering framework across N2, N3, and REM sleep stages: Stable (Cluster 0), Burden (Cluster 1), and High risk (Cluster 2). Compared with the Stable phenotype, the High-risk phenotype was consistently associated with increased cardiovascular risk, with the strongest association observed for incident CVD in the N2 stage [hazard ratio (HR) 1.468, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.280-1.684, P < 0.001]. Similar associations were observed in the N3 (HR 1.426, 95% CI 1.249-1.629, P < 0.001) and REM (HR 1.394, 95% CI 1.216-1.598, P < 0.001) stages. Sequential adjustment for AHI, oxygen desaturation index, arousal index, and sleep efficiency resulted in only minimal attenuation of hazard estimates, indicating that the prognostic associations were largely independent of conventional respiratory severity measures. In contrast, the Burden phenotype was consistently associated with lower all-cause mortality across all three sleep stages (HR 0.83-0.85, all P < 0.001). Subgroup analyses stratified by OSA severity demonstrated broadly consistent prognostic associations across AHI strata. Incorporating sleep stage-specific HRV features into conventional clinical phenotyping provides complementary prognostic information beyond traditional respiratory severity metrics. HRV-informed phenotyping may improve long-term cardiovascular risk stratification in patients with OSA.

papers.title: Variable task difficulty with augmented sensory feedback for motor training in virtual reality.
papers.abstract: This study examined how motor task difficulty and augmented sensory feedback (ASF) modality influence task performance, physiological responses, and perceptual experience during virtual reality (VR)-based upper-limb motor training. Building on related brace- and VR-based ASF platforms previously examined in neurotypical and spinal cord injury cohorts, the long-term goal is to support neurorehabilitation-oriented adaptive VR training; however, the present study used neurotypical participants as an initial validation step. Fourteen right-handed neurotypical participants used a supportive upper-limb brace and surface electromyography (EMG) for myoelectric control of a virtual robotic arm in a two-dimensional tracking task. A 2 × 2 within-subject design crossed ASF modality (visual feedback versus visual + haptic feedback) with task difficulty (straight-line versus sinusoidal trajectory). Outcomes included normalized path length, task completion time, movement jerk, alpha- and beta-band electroencephalogram (EEG) power over motor cortex, heart rate, EMG amplitude, EMG-displacement-based virtual work, and perceptual ratings of agency, motivation, and utility. Short-term pre-to-post percentage changes were computed for each measure. VHF straight-line training produced the largest reductions in normalized path length (-4.69%) and completion time (-6.12%), whereas VHF sinusoid training produced the largest reductions in movement jerk (-5.67%) and virtual work (-13.33%). ASF modality affected path length, completion time, jerk, EMG amplitude, and virtual work, whereas task difficulty modulated beta-band EEG power and the physiological index. Changes in path length were positively associated with changes in completion time and EMG amplitude. These findings suggest that ASF modality and task difficulty can differentially shape short-term behavioral, physiological, and perceptual responses in healthy participants. The exploratory distribution of participant-specific best-case conditions motivates future studies using independent trial subsets to evaluate whether behavioral and physiological measures can support individualized VR training.

papers.title: Nutritional status, health literacy, and lifestyle factors associated with health-related quality of life in patients with decompensated cirrhosis: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Liver cirrhosis is one of the leading causes of liver-related mortality worldwide. The disease typically progresses from an initially asymptomatic, compensated phase to decompensation, which adversely affects patients' health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Identifying the factors that influence HRQoL and implementing effective interventions are essential for improving patient outcomes. Based on the health ecology theory, this study focuses on health literacy and nutritional status, with the aim of enhancing patients' quality of survival through targeted interventions. A cross-sectional design was employed, using convenience sampling to recruit 202 patients with decompensated cirrhosis. Data collection included demographic information, biochemical indicators, and scores on health literacy, nutritional status, and HRQoL. Using IBM SPSS Statistics version 27, correlation analysis and multiple linear regression were conducted to primarily explore the associations of nutritional status, health literacy, and lifestyle factors with HRQoL. Correlation analysis showed that health literacy, nutritional status, sleep quality, and physical activity were significantly associated with patients' quality of life. Multiple linear regression revealed that nutritional status was independently associated with the HRQoL; notably, the model's explanatory power for HRQoL significantly increased (R Square increment) when health literacy was introduced, indicating practical significance. Furthermore, regression analyses showed that communication ability (B = -0.177, p = 0.007), walking (B = -1.589, p = 0.007), and aerobic exercise (B = -1.739, p = 0.017) as significant predictors of the physical dimension. Poor sleep significantly predicted both dimensions (physical: B = 1.193, p = 0.032; psychological: B = 0.532, p = 0.001), while information acquisition ability (B = -0.028, p = 0.021) specifically predicted the psychological dimension. This study demonstrated that both health literacy and nutritional status were significantly associated with the HRQoL among patients with decompensated cirrhosis. These findings may inform the design of targeted interventions to enhance health literacy and nutritional status, which may be beneficial for promoting self-management and improving clinical outcomes. Furthermore, they support the development of individualized management strategies.

papers.title: Birth of the Nigerian Sleep Society: A Milestone for Sleep Medicine in Nigeria and Africa.
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders are significant and are of major public health concern with high socioeconomic impact. However, they are under-recognised and under-treated in Nigeria and most of Africa, because of poor access to sleep specialists, sleep studies and limited treatment options. Prior to the inauguration of the Nigerian Sleep Society in 2025, there was no formal framework for sleep professionals in West Africa. Activities were on community engagement, awareness campaigns, meetings and scientific discussions on sleep health-related topical issues, training programs, collaborations, and publication of sleep health data, applicable to sub-Saharan Africa. Following the inauguration, the society is strategically positioned to address the critical barriers specifically affecting sleep medicine in West Africa, such as low community awareness, high costs of care, limited diagnostic capacity, insufficient training programs, inadequate sleep specialists, non-structured sleep health curriculum for undergraduates and postgraduates, lack of certification of sleep medicine personnel and inadequate research data. In this article, we explored the epidemiology of sleep disorder, the need for the Nigerian Sleep Society, its historical perspectives, and the strategic vision for addressing sleep disorders and the future pathway for sleep medicine in Nigeria and Africa.

papers.title: Comparative effects of exercise modalities on sleep quality in middle-aged and older adults with sleep disorders: A systematic review with pairwise, network, and dose-responsemeta-analyses.
papers.abstract: Exercise may improve sleep quality in middle-aged and older adults with sleep disorders, but the comparative effects of different exercise modalities and the dose-response relationship remain unclear. We systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception to May 2026. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials examining the effects of exercise interventions on sleep quality in middle-aged and older adults with sleep disorders. Two independent reviewers assessed study quality, and random-effects pairwise, network, and dose-response meta-analyses were performed to evaluate the effects of different exercise interventions and doses on sleep quality. The analysis included 23 randomized controlled trials involving 1,478 middle-aged and older adults with sleep disorders. Pairwise meta-analysis showed that exercise reduced Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) scores but had no significant effect on Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) scores. Bayesian network meta-analysis showed that, compared with the control group, aerobic exercise (SMD = 1.34, 95% CrI: 0.86∼1.82), mind-body exercise (SMD = 0.64, 95% CrI: 0.30∼0.97), and combined exercise (SMD = 0.60, 95% CrI: 0.13∼1.07) may improve PSQI scores. The dose-response analysis suggested an inverted U-shaped association, with the largest predicted effect occurring near 539 MET-min/week within the observed dose range. Low-to moderate-certainty evidence suggests that aerobic, mind-body, and combined exercise may reduce PSQI scores, with a nonlinear dose-response relationship.
papers.journal: Journal of exercise science and fitness

papers.title: Fetal and neonatal outcomes of pregnancies complicated by maternal sleep-disordered breathing: a systematic review.
papers.abstract: Maternal obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and the broader spectrum of sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) during pregnancy may be associated with fetal and neonatal outcomes, but the literature is heterogeneous and uses clinically distinct exposure definitions. This systematic review aimed to evaluate associations between maternal SDB and fetal/neonatal outcomes while preserving differences in exposure ascertainment. Following PRISMA 2020, the review was re-audited using updated PubMed and Web of Science searches, backward and forward citation searching, and ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP registry searches. Exposures were classified as (1) objectively confirmed OSA/SDB, (2) administrative-code-defined OSA, and (3) symptom-, snoring-, or questionnaire-defined SDB risk. No meta-analysis was conducted because clinically comparable subsets were insufficient for quantitative pooling. The completed re-audit identified 64 eligible publications mapped to 53 conservative cohort/dataset families (55 if two probable overlap pairs are treated as separate): 22 objective/physiologic, 11 administrative/clinical, and 31 symptom/questionnaire publications. Objective studies showed mixed findings, with fetal-growth or neonatal signals in selected cohorts but null findings in several other objectively assessed populations. Administrative-code OSA was repeatedly associated with preterm birth and selected neonatal outcomes, although exposure misclassification and residual confounding remain important. Symptom/questionnaire studies were heterogeneous, with associations varying by symptom definition, timing, and outcome. Current evidence does not establish a consistent fetal or neonatal risk pattern for objectively confirmed maternal OSA/SDB. Administrative-code and symptom/questionnaire evidence suggests associations for selected outcomes, particularly preterm birth, but should not be interpreted as a single homogeneous OSA effect. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420251110706.

papers.title: Validation and modification of a Chinese smell identification test (CSIT-12) in patients with Parkinson's disease and rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder.
papers.abstract: To enhance olfactory screening for Chinese patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) or rapid-eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) by developing and modifying a Chinese Smell Identification Test 12 (CSIT-12). In a discovery cohort, 69 PD patients and 47 healthy controls (HCs) were tested on 24 distinct odors using the Sniffin' Sticks Screening Test 12 (SSST-12) and CSIT-12. The 12 odors with the highest area under the curve (AUC) were selected to construct the Chinese version of the Sniffin' Sticks Screening Test 12 (C-SSST-12). This newly developed test was then validated in an independent cohort comprising 48 PD patients, 48 RBD patients, and 48 HCs. The reliability and validity of SSST-12, CSIT-12, C-SSST-12, and further abbreviated odor subsets were compared. Scores on SSST-12, CSIT-12, and C-SSST-12 were significantly lower in both PD and RBD compared to HCs (all P < 0.001). Both the CSIT-12 and SSST-12 demonstrated good discriminative capacity for PD versus HCs (CSIT-12: AUC = 0.832, sensitivity = 77.1%, specificity = 83.3%; SSST-12: AUC = 0.913, sensitivity = 85.4%, specificity = 81.3%) and RBD versus HCs (CSIT-12: AUC = 0.881, sensitivity = 85.4%, specificity = 83.3%; SSST-12: AUC = 0.893, sensitivity = 79.2%, specificity = 81.3%). Notably, the C-SSST-12 achieved the highest discriminative performance for PD versus HCs (AUC = 0.930, sensitivity = 81.3%, specificity = 85.4%) and RBD versus HCs (AUC = 0.949, sensitivity = 89.6%, specificity = 85.4%). A 5-odor CSIT-12 subset and a 3-odor C-SSST-12 subset retained high discriminative validity. This study highlights the discriminative value of utilizing culturally familiar odors for the screening of PD and RBD in Chinese populations. Furthermore, the abbreviated odor subsets offer highly efficient, rapid screening options suitable for community-based testing and fast-paced clinical environments.

papers.title: Aging in Autism: An Event-Related Potentials Study of Auditory Change Detection.
papers.abstract: Autistic individuals are often thought to exhibit reduced tolerance for change, which may stem from atypicalities in sensory processing, particularly in the detection of environmental changes. Within the predictive coding framework, this intolerance may reflect altered generation and updating internal predictions in response to sensory input, leading to increased prediction errors. Mismatch negativity and the P3a component are event-related potentials (ERPs) indexing automatic auditory change detection and involuntary attention shift. While studied in autistic children and young adults, little is known about how these components evolve during aging, an important gap as 21 million autistic adults over 60 are expected by 2050. This study examined mismatch negativity and P3a responses in 43 autistic adults (aged 21-64) and 60 nonautistic adults (aged 20-69) using a passive auditory oddball paradigm with standard (1000 Hz) and deviant (1100 Hz; p = 0.15) tones. Electroencephalography recording revealed no significant differences between autistic and nonautistic individuals on mismatch negativity and P3a amplitude or latency. However, mismatch negativity amplitude decreased with age over frontal site, similarly across both groups. No age-related effects were found for mismatch negativity latency or P3a measures in either group. These findings suggest that, from adulthood onward, the neural mechanisms underlying automatic change detection and preattentional processes are similar in both autistic and nonautistic adults, and that their overall time course of aging appears comparable, supporting the parallel aging hypothesis. Nonetheless, future research should explore how these preserved neural responses relate to behavioral reactivity to change in autism.

papers.title: Pre-sleep milk-derived proteins do not impair sleep or recovery in elite female athletes.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for athlete recovery and performance, yet athletes frequently experience restricted or poor-quality sleep. Pre-sleep feeding (PSF) has emerged as a strategy to support recovery, but randomized, double-blinded, crossover trials comparing PSF macronutrient options on objective and subjective sleep outcomes in elite female athletes remain limited. Twenty-five National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I female athletes (18-25 years old) were recruited; 21 completed the trial. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo controlled, crossover design conducted over 4-8 weeks, participants consumed four treatments for three consecutive nights each: 40 g casein protein (CAS; 160 kcal), 40 g α-lactalbumin protein (ALA; 160 kcal), 40 g carbohydrate (CHO; 160 kcal), and 40g of a placebo (PLA; 5 kcal), with a minimum three-day washout between conditions. Supplements were consumed ~2 h after the final meal and ~30 min before bedtime as the last caloric intake of the day. Objective outcomes were obtained from the WHOOP 4.0 device (total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), sleep efficiency (SE), resting heart rate (RHR), and heart rate variability (HRV)). Subjective outcomes were assessed each morning via questionnaires (subjective sleep quality (SSQ), subjective sleep onset latency (SSOL), and subjective recovery (SREC)). Nocturnal interstitial glucose was assessed via blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in a subset (n = 6). Sleep and recovery variables were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate treatment effects across the four supplementation conditions. For CGM data, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate main effects of treatment and time, as well as the treatment × time interaction. Tukey's post hoc testing was used with significance set at p < 0.05. No significant treatment effects were observed for TST, SOL, SE, RHR, or HRV (p > 0.05). TST ranged from 7.47-7.62 h, SE from 91.5-92.0%, RHR from 53.5-54.1 bpm, and HRV from 98.2-103.9 ms across conditions. No significant treatment effects were detected for SSQ, SSOL, or SREC (p > 0.05); SSQ ranged from 69-75%, SSOL from 16-20 min, and SREC from 61-66%. In the CGM sub-analysis, a main effect of time was observed for nocturnal glucose (p = 0.008), but no differences among treatments (p = 0.187) or a time × treatment interaction (p = 0.550) were detected. In NCAA Division I female athletes, three consecutive nights of pre-sleep ingestion of CAS, ALA, or CHO did not impair objective or subjective measures of sleep or recovery compared with PLA. These findings demonstrate that pre-sleep feeding, regardless of macronutrient type, can be incorporated without negatively affecting sleep quality or recovery metrics. papers.title: The effect of text-picture consistency on memory integration in college students: Evidence from ERPs.
papers.abstract: In multimedia learning, individuals often need to integrate textual and visual information. The neural mechanisms underlying how consistency between text and pictures affects memory integration remain unclear. To examine the effect of text-picture consistency on memory integration in college students and to determine the processing time at which this effect occurs. Totally 28 Chinese college students (nfemale = 20, nmale = 8; Mage = 21.64 ± 2.30) participated in this experiment. An adapted pictorial demonstration paradigm was employed. Participants sequentially learned two pairs of text-picture stem facts (consistent vs. inconsistent), separated by an interval, followed by a recognition test for stem and integrated facts. Behavioural and event-related potential (ERP) data were recorded simultaneously. Under the text-picture consistency condition, college students showed significantly better memory integration performance than under the inconsistency condition (58% vs. 48%). EEG results showed that the text-picture inconsistency condition (i.e., the picture and text within a single stem fact were semantically mismatched) elicited a larger P600 wave (500-800 ms) than the text-picture consistency condition, suggesting that text-picture inconsistency primarily induces conflict and integration difficulties during late cognitive processing. No significant differences were observed in the early N400 component. Text-picture consistency facilitates memory integration primarily during late processing, aligning with cognitive theories of multimedia learning. Educationally, it serves as a key quality indicator for multimedia material design. Instructors should prioritize semantic alignment and assess knowledge integration during evaluation.
papers.journal: The British journal of educational psychology

papers.title: Clinical and Research Trends in Adult Acupressure Randomized Controlled Trials: A Scoping and Bibliometric Review.
papers.abstract: Acupressure has gained increasing attention as a noninvasive, low-risk, and cost-effective complementary intervention to address persistent symptoms such as pain, anxiety, fatigue, and sleep disturbances among adults. Although the volume of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating acupressure has grown substantially, an integrated synthesis that combines clinical evidence mapping with bibliometric characterization remains limited. This study aimed to conduct an integrated scoping review and bibliometric analysis of RCTs on acupressure interventions among adults in order to map the scope of clinical evidence and identify publication trends, thematic concentrations, and research collaboration patterns. This integrated scoping review was reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Extension for Scoping Reviews reporting guideline. RCTs published between 2020 and 2025 were retrieved from the Scopus database using Population-Concept-Context (PCC) eligibility criteria. The included studies involved adults aged 18 years or older who received acupressure interventions in clinical or health care settings. Data extraction captured both clinical characteristics and bibliometric indicators. Descriptive synthesis was integrated with bibliometric analyses of annual publication trends, subject areas, geographic distribution, author productivity, collaboration networks, and keyword co-occurrence. A total of 303 RCTs were included. Publication output increased steadily, with a notable surge after 2022. Most studies were indexed within Medicine and Nursing. China, Iran, and the United States were the most productive countries, while international collaboration remained limited. Thematic analysis revealed that pain and musculoskeletal conditions were the dominant focuses, closely linked to quality-of-life outcomes. Psychological symptoms and sleep disturbances formed a strongly interconnected cluster, alongside emerging applications in women's health and chronic disease management. The evidence base for adult acupressure has expanded rapidly and demonstrates increasing thematic coherence. Future research should prioritize broader collaboration, diversified clinical applications, and implementation-oriented studies to enhance the translation of findings into practice.
